Alongside it is a very opinionated Svelte UI library called Phoundry UI that was built specifically for Phials, including a 700+ hand crafted icon library.

Thanks for checking it out <3

story_text.value:
I love Civilization VI, and I've been playing since it came out a little over a decade ago. I decided to vibe code up a clone that can be played in the browser (currently playable up to the industrialization era)

I initially reproduced the game mechanics through a combination of memory and online sources, but that misses a huge amount of detail. I took inspiration from another project, civvis.ai. They used actual recordings of the game to get all the mechanics right. I have been dong the same, running through AI games to gather more recordings and make the mechanics more accurate, but there is still a long way to go! (Please let me know if you find inaccuracies)

My ultimate goal is to have an accurate recreation of the engine for myself and other hackers to mess around with. Particularly, I've been running AI agents through the game to see how they do, and whether they could make formidable opponents.

Please excuse the AI art - I am not an artist. I tried iterating on it a lot, but I could not fully dispose of that tell tale AI texture.

Enjoy~

story_text.value:
Hey HN! I'm Lakshay, and at Cerulion we cooked up a harness for physical AI. Built on top of our deterministic runtime, we now have MCP tools that let any LLM see and move a robot. It closes the loop with measurements so a model doesn't try to guess its way through the task, and imbues common sense and robotics best practices into the workflow.

We ran the numbers on LIBERO-PRO and quite frankly are a bit shocked. Gemini 3.8 Flash with Cerulion solved 73 of 100 LIBERO-PRO tasks. GPT-6 Astra on a bare 3-tool baseline (arXiv:2610.30051) solved 71, at about 12x the cost and 3x the wall time per run. Flash on that same baseline solved 25.

Guys. Gemini 3.8 Flash matched GPT-6 Astra for robotics. Model intelligence is not the bottleneck. A harness is all you need ;)

Star us and follow along. Try the quickstart, lmk what you guys wanna see next. I'll post again soon! (teaser: my Nespresso machine is getting a lot of attention from my robot arm)

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

I read HN every day and sometimes I wish I could just talk about a story with people instead of writing comments.

So I wanted to build this as an app.

You open a story, see if anyone is in there, tap and you're in. It's push to talk by default so it doesn't get chaotic, you can switch to open mic if you want.

You can keep reading the comments or lock your phone and the room keeps going.

No signup, you get a random name (or verify your HN username if you want). It's Flutter on the app side, Go backend, and I self host LiveKit for the audio conversations.

App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6504711182

Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.canerg.bet...

Rooms are empty unless people are in them obviously.

story_text.value:
I have been exploring a different future for AI where we can finally take control of our models and keep our data 100% private. I built modelXare with the goal of creating the DNS-equivalent for AI capabilities. It uses a combination of system one and system two models to dynamically route the user intent(s) to the ideal micro-model(s) that gets downloaded (and cached) locally to processes your request.

This is just the first iteration of this vision. There is a lot of work that needs to be done and a lot of micro-models that can be added but imagine a world where we all can build this network of micro-models together and break the chains from the big AI labs.

title.value: Show HN: ModelXare – Decentralized AI Models

story_text.value:
We built Hyper Elements. A open source content engine for agents. It lets them build emails, PDFs or images in React using much fewer tokens.

The agent writes content, our engine handles the layout and markup. It also tells the agent what the problems are in the content and how to fix them.

We tested it by giving Claude Code a brief and run it 5 times with different libraries like Hyper Elements, React Email and MJML. Each run, Hyper Elements used fewer tokens and produced a passing email much faster. The benchmark is also open source in the repo.

story_text.value:
Colin here, mostly known for creating Zod.

Reylo is a new open source project I'm working on that takes advantage of the new Content Mapper API in TypeScript 7.1 (currently still in beta). Content mappers are sort of like plugins for TypeScript in that they let you define loaders for external file types. My mind went straight to .sql.

This started as an experiment, but it's turned into a serious engineering effort.

• Support for Postgres, MySQL, and SQLite

• The inference engine is written in Rust. It relies on prepared queries to the greatest extent possible but augments from there with its own AST.

• The major JSON schema extensions for each dialect are natively supported (e.g. pg_jsonschema on Postgres), so JSON Schema CHECK constraints are reflected in the return types

• Type information bubbles up through JSON aggregation

• We have our own internal type definition spec ("Reylo Type Defs") that's sort of like JSON Schema but it can represent a superset of the type systems in all major RDBMSs. Still just an internal representation, but there are a lot of fun ideas in it for anyone who's interested in that kind of design space.

• Planning to add support for other languages beyond TypeScript soon, including a macro for Rust/sqlx

Docs are here[0] or you can play around with the inference in-browser using the playground[1] (locally runs PGlite and Reylo's WASM build).

[0] https://reylo.dev/docs [1] https://reylo.dev/play

title.value: Show HN: Reylo – Import .sql files into TypeScript with full type inference

story_text.value:
tl;dr: We just open-sourced Wakeshift, which lets any MCP server serve interoperable events via MCP Events or harness-specific bridges. This allows MCP servers to push events to harnesses that don't support MCP Events today, including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

Hi folks! The MCP Events spec was approved and merged five days ago, allowing MCP servers to emit events directly to agent subscribers. (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol...) This allows MCP developers to push events directly to agents for long-running tasks (e.g. CI, crawls, starting agents) or external actions (e.g. emails, human approvals, alerts).

However, the catch is that support for MCP Events is very light. Claude Code and Codex don't support it at all, and most of the implementations support the draft version rather than the merged spec. Many harnesses can work around this with plugins or hooks, but every MCP server has to build it for each harness.

Wakeshift provides interoperable events to your MCP server. You call emit() and Wakeshift pushes the event to each subscribed agent in whatever format they accept: per the MCP Events final spec, an earlier draft, or through a hook / plugin where needed. If the harness requires a hook / plugin and it's not already installed, the agent will be notified and receive instructions on how to install it for the user.

Additionally, the MCP Events spec defines three delivery mechanisms: webhook, push (via held HTTP request) and pull (via HTTP polling). The Wakeshift SDK serves push and poll from your MCP server, so agents that can't accept inbound HTTP webhooks (e.g. most agents running on laptops) can still get events within seconds.

Subscriptions only start when an agent calls a tool that subscribes it, and users can list or stop them anytime. Some harnesses can only be woken by putting a message into the conversation, so Wakeshift wraps the content as an external event to reduce the risk of prompt injection.

The repo linked has a quickstart guide to get this working locally in a few minutes. Or you can try our hosted webhook service to test it yourself without an installation. (https://try.wakeshift.ai)

We'd love feedback, PRs for harnesses we don't cover, reports when it doesn't work. As you can imagine, there's a combinatorial explosion of servers, harnesses, models, OSs, etc. so we expect there to be some rough edges. Are there any MCP servers you're using that you think could benefit from having events today?

title.value: Show HN: Wakeshift – Open-Source MCP Events for Claude Code, Codex and More

story_text.value:
I originally started building Mole as an open-source tool a couple of months ago, because I was annoyed with my LLMs returning super confident answers to my questions about facts, numbers, statistics, etc. They basically recited big claims from news articles, about which I'm naturally skeptical. And of course, once I manually traced a few of these to their sources, they turned out to be subpar, or downright incorrect.

So I came up with Mole, a tool that searches and reads sources, extracts claims, checks each against a verbatim quote from the page, and flags disagreements between the sources.

The OS version just got v0.3.0 released today, the biggest feature of this release is that it now tries to go all the way through the very origin of a statistic to see where it originally came from.

Besides this, the hosted version runs the OS core, but it researches any question for you without installing anything, and creates a clean, downloadable research report that you can carry with you into a business meeting, an academic presentation, or any such place. Hope you find it useful and leave me some feedback!

story_text.value:
I've been building websites for agencies for over a decade. Much of the review process has involved simply sharing the staging site with the client for review, along with the password to view if it's password protected for viewing purposes. The client sends an email back with the requested changes listed out in the email, or in an attached file like a PDF of Excel spreadsheet. Or the agency uses an online proofing service like Ziflow or something similar for the internal team to review and make changes, and then they share that with the client so they can review.

This could be a bit of a mess if it's all through PDF comments, or a chain of emails, or in some Excel file. Even with a proofing service it could be a hassle. In the case of a proofing service, maybe they don't have a capture tool like this and you have to resort to using the FireShot extension or some other capture tool, and then combine them into a single doc to upload for review using yet another tool somewhere.

With all this in mind, I wanted to create my own version of this that offers a bit more. The Stetup capture tool takes a list of URLs, or a site's sitemap, and captures a full-page screenshot of each page, and then returns a single combined PDF with every page. Before each capture it flattens sticky headers and other sticky elements, it opens accordions, and hides cookie banners. You can choose desktop, mobile, or your own screen's width. You can drop in PDFs you already have, and reorder them among the pages you're capturing.

It also works on staging sites that are password protected. You enter the password to view your staging site (and username if it's needed, e.g. WP Engine). The info you enter will be used for that job only and will be deleted when the job is complete. If the site has a pop-up that asks who you are before showing the page, you can provide the button's text and it will be clicked before each page capture.

Under the hood it's headless Chromium in a worker. The URLs are checked against private and internal addresses, and the worker accesses the internet through a filtering proxy. All files are deleted after 24 hours. It's free, no account is required, and you can do 10 URLs or PDFs per job, and 3 jobs an hour.

It's part of a review tool I am creating called Stetup that's for agencies and their clients. And the full-page captures of real sites probably have some edge cases I haven't considered, so I'd appreciate all the feedback I can get.

story_text.value:
Hey HN!

I'm the cofounder and CEO at Baseshift, where we create branchable DB snapshots using a bespoke libc for databases. We use this infra to research novel lossless compression codecs of database pages, including neural models.

We're sharing some recent results. You can download pre-built, dockerized US & NY OpenStreetMap PostgreSQL with compression ratios of 8.5 and 8.94 respectively. The data in the images remains compressed while in use, and allows for 8KB random read access, for example:

  # downloads about 1.55 GB
  docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 baseshift/db-osm-ny
  psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres -d osm_new_york_261024
You can download the whole US OpenStreetMap with baseshift/db-osm-us (240GB -> 28GB). There's also a variety of synthetic/generated databases with varying sizes: Nick's Gaming Emporium, https://nge-data.com/ at baseshift/db-nge-[tiny|small|medium]

For US/NY we've surpassed zpaq -m5 on whole database files, while maintaining 8kb random reads and <1.5ms decode times on a single CPU core with standard C.

Our codecs are designed to leverage parallel compute optimizations in the CPU when they're available. For example, with AVX-512 VNNI our single core decode times reduce from ~1.4ms to ~180us.

We will be uploading the remaining ~190 OSM countries and 53 US states/territories in the coming days.

I plan on posting a proper paper to arXiv in the coming weeks, but would be great to get the community's thoughts.

story_text.value:
I vibe coded Webtools, a collection of everyday web utilities that runs completely offline inside the browser.

Why? every time I needed to sign a pdf, delete pages from a pdf, or convert image formats or resize them, I found myself having to upload files to random websites which uploads these file to their servers, at least temporally. I wanted a clean single place for these utilities where user privacy is guaranteed by design.

Webtools has zero backend or tracking, processing happens completely in the browser. it's built with React and Tailwind CSS, and is packaged as a PWA so it works completely offline on any device that has a browser.
